paras: The Pike County whitecapping campaign of 1903 was a series of threats and attacks by a band of white men against Black tenants, laborers and churches in the Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of Troy, Alabama. Notices threatening death drove off the hands of a sawmill and several farms, houses were shot into, a woman and her baby were wounded, and two Black churches were burned. Six white farmers were arrested by federal officers in October 1903, and five were indicted in January 1904 for oppressing Black residents because of their race.

According to the federal indictments, the oppression ran from early 1902 until September 1903, when the government took up the matter. A Troy correspondent wrote that hostility toward Black people in Cross Roads Beat had led to "two or three personal conflicts." The targets included tenants of James Daniels and James Phenix and the mostly Black workers of a steam sawmill owned by R. J. Williams and his son Lon.

In April 1903 a Black farm hand, Will Sewell, was tied and whipped with a wagon whip so severely that he could not work for three weeks; a witness said he was whipped "as a medicine and tonic." Joe Browning, a Black renter, received a notice enclosed in a miniature coffin, and when he did not leave, his house was shot into at night. Mary Clements's house was riddled with shot, and she and the baby in her arms were hit as she fled, though neither was very seriously wounded.

On September 7, 1903, a notice signed "The W. C. of I. and C." told Garfield Williams, a tenant of Daniels, to go twenty-five miles away within five days or "death will be your portion," and he left. Phenix's tenants were warned soon after, and the whole crew of the Williams mill was told to leave or be killed; so many fled that the mill shut down. Most notices were signed "Negro Skinner," and two Black churches, Dunn's Chapel and Antioch, were burned.

In September the sheriff searched the area for clues, and the Advertiser expected an inquiry by the county grand jury, whose foreman was the mill owner R. J. Williams. No report of county grand jury action was found; federal agents gathered evidence, and on October 27 a deputy U.S. marshal arrested Boss Riley, William Pittman, Tumps Chesser and Robert, John and Fletcher Windham.

At a preliminary hearing before U.S. Commissioner Tutwiler at Troy on October 30 and 31, some twenty-five or thirty government witnesses, both white and Black, testified before a large crowd. The commissioner discharged Robert Windham and held the other five for the federal grand jury, Fletcher Windham on $750 bail and the rest on $500.

In January 1904 the federal grand jury at Montgomery indicted Riley, Pittman and the three Windhams for attempting to oppress ten named Black people, Browning and Clements among them, "because they are of African descent." The cases were set for the May term, and the coverage does not show their outcome.

The Montgomery Advertiser covered the case through specials from Troy, first under the headline "NEGROES THREATENED," blaming a "lawless element." Its hearing report described "rather startling conditions" and said the county's "best element" opposed such crimes because they hurt farming. Papers in Indianapolis, Atlanta and Goldsboro ran only brief wires on the arrests; the New-York Tribune headed its indictment story "BLACKS CAUGHT IT HARD."

In November the St. Paul Appeal printed a Birmingham dispatch as "A TALE OF HORROR" in its column "Caucasian Crookedness," meant to show there was "no color line in crime," and the Professional World headed its brief "Alabama Negro Outrages." Both Black papers put the number who fled the county at 150 or more, a figure absent from the white reports.

The Professional World said Mary Clements's baby was killed, while the Advertiser's report of the hearing testimony and the New-York Tribune's account of the indictments describe the baby as shot and wounded. The St. Paul Appeal alone said Browning was beaten so badly that he lay near death for a day; the local reports and the indictments mention only the shooting into his house.

reader.title: Pike County whitecapping campaign of 1903
bases: A band signing notices 'Negro Skinner' and 'W. C. J. and C.' ordered Black tenants and mill hands to leave on pain of death, shot into houses, whipped men and burned churches, and its accused members were charged with whitecapping (A1, A6, A9, A14).

The local Montgomery Advertiser specials (A1, A6, A9), the federal indictments reported in A14 and A15, and two Black-press accounts (A12, A13) agree on the core campaign of notices, shootings and church burnings, though A13 differs on whether the baby died.

accounts.gist: Whitecappers in Cross Roads Beat posted death-threat notices, shot into Browning's house, and drove off farm tenants and the Williams mill hands; the sheriff was investigating.

accounts.label: Government witnesses at the preliminary hearing
accounts.gist: Churches were burned, Black residents whipped and warned off, Browning's house shot into, and Mary Clements and her baby shot as they fled; neither was very seriously wounded.

accounts.label: Federal indictments
accounts.gist: Five men conspired from early 1902 to September 1903 to oppress ten named Black people because of their race, burning two churches and firing into the houses of Browning and Clements.

accounts.label: Black press summary
accounts.gist: The Appeal said Browning was badly beaten and Clements riddled with bullets and that 150 left the county; the Professional World said the baby was killed.

framing.detail: The Advertiser headed the first report 'NEGROES THREATENED' and blamed a 'lawless element', later describing 'rather startling conditions' and the opposition of 'the best element' as a matter of farming interests.
Out-of-state papers ran short wires on the arrests ('Alleged Whitecappers Arrested') and the indictments ('BLACKS CAUGHT IT HARD').
The St. Paul Appeal placed the story under 'CAUCASIAN CROOKEDNESS' as 'A TALE OF HORROR' to show that 'there is no color line in crime'; the Professional World called it 'Alabama Negro Outrages'.

record_check.dossier: whitecapping: a band drove Black tenants and workers away; no forced labor is reported. The 'peonage' brief (A3) concerns a different Troy case.
Sept. 7, 1903 is the date of one notice (to Garfield Williams); the campaign ran from early 1902 to September 1903 per the indictments.
Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of Troy; Troy was the dateline and hearing site.
Joe Browning and at least nine other named Black people (Mary Clements, Garfield Williams, Josh Toney, Elisha Leverette, five mill employees), plus Will Sewell and two churches.
ordered_out, threats of death, shooting into houses, shooting and wounding, whipping, church burning; no forced labor or work action.
Six white farmers accused: Boss Riley, Will Pittman, Tumps Chesser, Robert, John and Fletcher Windham.
At least two (Mary Clements and her baby) shot; Will Sewell and 'five or six' others whipped.
Coverage ran to Jan. 29, 1904, including arrests, hearing and indictments, and two Black papers (St. Paul Appeal, Professional World).

info: A campaign of threats and violence; the indictments fixed the oppression from early 1902 to September 1903. Browning's house was shot into 'some time ago' before Sept. 11; Garfield Williams's notice was dated Sept. 7, 1903; Phenix's tenants were warned about Sept. 9-10; Will Sewell was whipped in April 1903.
Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of Troy, Pike County

Joe Browning; Mary Clements and her baby; Garfield Williams (tenant of James Daniels); Josh Toney (laborer for James Phenix/Phoenix); Elisha Leverette; William Sherman, General Boyd, James Knight, Elbert Dixon and J. C. Collins (employees of Alonzo/Lon Williams's mill); Will Sewell (whipped); the congregations of Dunn's Chapel and Antioch

No accusation against the victims was reported; the notices simply ordered them to leave. A9 reports Sewell was whipped 'as a medicine and tonic' and that the mill hands were described as 'quiet inoffensive negroes'.

Accused: Boss Riley, Will (William) Pittman/Pitman, Tumps Chesser, Robert Windham, John Windham and Fletcher Windham, white farmers living about twelve miles from Troy; described as an 'organized gang'
None, per the Advertiser and Tribune; the Professional World said the baby was killed
Five held for the federal grand jury (Fletcher Windham on $750 bail, the others $500); Robert Windham discharged
